title: Making and using joining slip
subtitle: Preparing the clay-and-water slurry that bonds clay pieces together
excerpt: Joining slip is a thick slurry of clay and water used to attach clay elements: handles to cups, slabs to walls, coils to bases. Without it, pressed-together clay joints open when the piece dries. This tutorial covers making joining slip from your clay body and using score-and-slip correctly every time.
sourceNotes: Score-and-slip joining methodology is foundational to hand-building ceramics. Documented across all major hand-building instruction sources.

content.text: Clay joints fail when the pieces dry at different rates and pull apart. Joining
slip
applied between
scored

surfaces creates a mechanical and chemical bond that matches the shrinkage of both pieces because it is made from the same clay body. The slip works by slipping wet clay particles between the rough scratched surfaces of both pieces, welding them together as they dry.
Making joining slip

Collect scraps of the same clay body you are building with: leftover trimming scraps, dried bits, or offcuts. Joining slip must be made from the same clay as the pieces being joined, because different clay bodies shrink at different rates and create stress at the joint.
Place the scraps in a jar and cover with water. Leave overnight for dry scraps; fresh scraps soften in one to two hours. The clay dissolves into the water to form a slurry.

The right consistency for joining is similar to thick cream: it coats the brush and holds briefly before dripping. Too thin (like milk) and it does not provide enough clay matter for the bond. Too thick (like toothpaste) and it traps air at the joint.
Store in a sealed jar. Joining slip keeps indefinitely; if it separates, stir before use. If it dries out, add a few drops of water and stir.
Score-and-slip method
Bring both surfaces to
leather-hard

before joining. Leather-hard is the correct joining stage: the clay is firm enough to hold its shape but soft enough to absorb the joining slip and form a bond. Bone-dry clay cannot be reliably joined with slip.

Score both surfaces to be joined with a needle tool, fork, or pointed knife: crosshatch scratches about 5 mm apart across the full joining area. The scratches give the slip somewhere to grip mechanically.
Apply joining slip to both scored surfaces with a brush, covering the scratched area completely. The slip should go into the scratches, not just sit on top.

Press the two surfaces together and hold for 30 seconds. Excess slip should squeeze out around the joint: wipe away. Smooth over the joint from the inside with a finger, blending the clay on either side into the joint rather than just spreading slip across the surface.
Support the joint while drying if needed: prop, tape, or fill to prevent sag. Check the joint after two hours: if any gap has opened, re-apply slip while still damp.
Common mistakes
Joint opens during drying: clay too dry when joined; slip too thin. Join at leather-hard, use thicker slip, and blend the inside of the joint with a finger.
Slip applied only to one side: both surfaces must be scored and slipped. Slip on one surface only is a common cause of joint failure.
Slip made from a different clay body: the different shrinkage rate creates a stress crack exactly at the joint. Always use the same clay to make the slip.

rows.problem: Hairline crack exactly at the join after drying
rows.cause: Pieces at different moisture stages when joined; or slip from mismatched clay body
rows.fix: Join only at matching moisture levels. Make the slip from the same clay body as the piece.

rows.problem: Slip dried too fast on the surface before pressing
rows.cause: Working in a dry environment; pieces leather-hard but drying further as you prepare
rows.fix: Cover pieces with a damp cloth while preparing the second piece for joining. Re-wet the scored surface lightly with a damp brush before applying slip.
